previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, COPD, and alcohol dependence was admitted for chest pain, bilateral foot pain, and suprapubic pain after losing his medications and being homeless. He presented with sharp, non-exertional chest pain and elevated BNP, indicating heart failure exacerbation, managed with IV furosemide and reinitiation of home heart failure medications. His chest pain was determined to be atypical and non-ischemic, with normal EKGs and negative troponins. Bilateral foot pain, related to prior amputations and neuropathy, was evaluated with X-rays showing no osteomyelitis but possible gout-related changes; podiatry recommended non-opioid pain management with tramadol and Lyrica. Suprapubic pain following a recent GI bleed was assessed with ultrasound, which ruled out hernia, and he was discharged on omeprazole. He expressed readiness to stop drinking, was monitored for withdrawal with CIWA and thiamine, and was connected with social work for shelter placement and sobriety resources. He was discharged home with all home medications, including rivaroxaban, metoprolol, and inhalers, and a follow-up appointment.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you at ___. You came into the 
hospital with symptoms of shortness of breath, chest pain and 
feeling like your abdomen was distended. Your initial EKG, CXR 
and tests did not show any evidence of a heart attack. For your 
symptoms it was thought to be from either a lung infection 
causing COPD exacerbation or from fluid overload from not taking 
your regular medications. You were given antibiotics, steroids 
and nebulizers to treat any component of COPD exacerbation and 
also restarted on your all of your home medications to get rid 
of the extra fluid. On this therapy you had big improvements! 
You got rid of 5 liters of extra fluid and also had a decrease 
in your abdominal distension with resolution of all your 
symptoms.

In addition, you had an ultrasound of your heart done which 
showed some changes to your heart from your last ultrasound. For 
this you should be sure to talk with a primary care doctor and 
talk about any changes to your treatment. 

Finally, you had to get valium while in the hospital for 
potential alcohol withdraw. You did not have a seizure or any 
significant symptoms at the time of discharge, but it is 
important that you continue to get help with this problem and 
stop drinking as alcohol is contributing in a major way to your 
health problems.
